en: A single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold; a single word of ultimate truth transmutes the mundane into the sacred.
Only the venerable monk who has attained self-realization received the golden robe from the ancient Buddha Hongzhi and held the staff of authority within the hall of Jingci.

He may truly be called the single wheel among the myriad stars and the solitary vessel among the ten thousand things. As for those who rely on tortoise shells and divining stalks— [The text ends here.]
The spring colors of Dongshan are like a clear mirror suspended over the *Zhongxu* (Continued) collection of the Indian land. Water conforms to square and round;
the Way unites the ordinary and the sage. I hope that those who read this book will understand it as a small supplement, rather than something intended to harmonize with broad faith.
When the Layman Fenglin Xiuyu was serving as the Governor of Wenzhou, he first encountered this marvelous record. He respectfully expresses his conviction and aspiration. Wanshou.

What Master Zhanxi has recorded here is most worthy of being appended as a report on the grace of the Dharma; it is truly marvelous and extraordinary. It must not be treated lightly; I respectfully transcribe it.
These are jade from Jing, pearls from Li, elegant speech, and golden words. To know them is called being wise; to hold fast to them is called being a sage. Furthermore, regarding this collection...
These words are most rare indeed. This wondrously luminous ground has been personally revealed by the Master himself in golden verses;

this place where the spiritual source is realized is like a polished pearl-texture that brings forth clear radiance. As I, Yu, reverently read them in my humble chamber, the jade and pearls shine brilliantly upon the sandalwood platter.

Whether it be light or dark, the true lamp itself is free from light and darkness; whether it be clear or turbid, the water of the nature is fundamentally devoid of clarity or murkiness. Only then can one truly believe.

A single word on the Way cannot repay a ten-thousand-year debt of grace; three lifetimes are easily understood, yet the heart of a thousand ages is profound. I have selected these clumsy verses and have ventured to inscribe them at the beginning.
Written respectfully by the monk Donggu Miaoguang, a successor of the Patriarchs residing at Lingyin.

Illustrations. There was a man of benevolence in the Great Tang; his surname was Yu, and he was the grandson of Grand Master Yuan.

Yet, taking up ancient chapters and words, he has brought them forth here. Now, reading these writings, he is truly an extraordinary sage. Relying on the categories of calligraphic usage, one observes his revisions.

On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and, raising his whisk, said: "The celestial canopy is clear; the sea vessel floats afar. The mountain oarsman stands high."
The riverbed is exhausted of its wonders; it is exactly so. Where is the man who possesses the eye? After a long silence, he said: "At night, the crane dreams of purity;
the whale’s snout is cold. By day, the owl’s spirit stirs; the hawk’s feathers grow thin. Tell me, is there any news at the beginning of the new year?
Holding up his whisk, he said: "Look, look! The richness of the stone-flower grass, the spirit of the herb."
Shishuang Zong said: "When seeing the sun and moon, why do you ask? The heavens are the sail; the four seas are the boat.
It is exposed and exposed, majestic and grand. The mountains are the oars, the heights are lofty, and the rivers and marshes exhaust the mystery."

Ten thousand mountains serve as oars; a thousand rivers form a marsh. The scholar is lofty, leaping directly forward in a single bound. The ultimate subtlety is perfectly clear within its own station.
Precisely at such a moment, the Way of Ruler and Subject is harmonized. Where is the man with eyes? Can you see it with your own eyes in this secret place?
After a long silence, he said: "From of old, no one has understood it. The night crane dreams of the pure whale."
The beak is cold; it has already become biased, yet it is not yet biased. By day the owl’s spirit stirs, while the hawk’s feathers grow thin.
Principle turns into affairs, yet affairs are not yet affairs. Although this is so, those who know the sound are few. But tell me, is there still news at the beginning of the new year?
Ancient matters change their hue; present matters gain their freshness. The hundred flowers are rich and noble, and the grasses possess spirit. Furthermore—
"How is it? This is a living phrase. He said in a small public sermon:
"On the mountain, beyond the railing; beneath the water, before the balustrade. At night, the hare’s light is snow; by day, the crow’s brilliance is fire."
Huangtou produced the sublime; Vimalakīrti entered the profound. The Hu monk sealed his mind; Master Lu transmitted the robe. Zhang San’s rustic air; Li Si’s woodcutter’s song.
The boat moves through the azure waves; the sea drenches the solitary sky. In the ultimate sense, there is suchness—tread this path in this very way.
Regarding this single shout, it is said: "The three sections are not the same. Changshou said:
"On the mountain, beyond the railing; beneath the water, before the balustrade. The light of the night hare upon the snow; the breath of the day crow like fire.
By means of these four lines, he elucidates the matters prior to when even a single Buddha had appeared in the world, or when a single Patriarch had yet emerged. Huangtou—
"Producing the wondrous, entering the profound purity of the Vimalakīrti; the Hu monk [Bodhidharma] sealing the mind, and Master Lu [Hui-neng] transmitting the robe.

By these four lines, one understands the matter of all Buddhas appearing in the world and the reason for the patriarchs' coming from the West. It is like the rustic songs of Zhang San and the woodcutter's chants of Li Si."
The boat moves across the blue-green waves; the sea submerges the solitary sky. With these four lines, [the Master] enlightened Beidou to board his original vessel.
Casting the line and grasping the fishing rod—these three stages are not the same; a monk of the fundamental lineage must investigate them.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, he ascended the hall and said: "On this fifteenth day of the month of *zhōu*, the wind blows; At the mountain peak, snowy vapors bind the cold pines.
I know not what news the withered tree has received, Yet the numinous flower containing jade blooms within a spring dream.

Auspicious birds fly forth across ten thousand peaks; Prophetic fish swim past the assembly of two or three. In the midst of this bustle, they meet before the Master’s eyes— Clearly, distinctly, a pair."
His eyes penetrate everywhere. Shuang said:
"With a thousand hands and eyes wide open, one attains the three clarities and six supernatural powers. Whatever is grasped by the hand is acceptable;
whatever is discerned at will is exquisite. This is a brief summary of the discourse on entering the hall; you should see it as it applies to the present time."
The interplay of the partial and the primary is as stated in the *Small Public Sermon*: "The spring breeze blows through the night pavilion; the fragrance of plum blossoms fills one's robes.
By whose grace and power is this? A dim moon crosses the river at night; a monkey drifts through the mountain peaks. Whose livelihood is this? Cut off all manifold distinctions."
This is the crossroads where the wind and moon of a single morning reach their end. Is there even a distinction between Buddhas and patriarchs here? Please try to judge this for me. Shuang said:
"Seeking people, one unconsciously scoops up mud and water; turning toward the sun, one only then knows how to receive its warmth. What is this?
Human kindness and power: flaws give birth to jade; the sharp edge reveals the sword. Whose livelihood is this?

To humble oneself to serve others, to suppress the worthy to make them lowly—is there even a trace of this within the domain of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Heaven is high, yet one does not look up at it;
earth is vast, yet one does not tread upon it. Nevertheless, without possessing these eyes, how can one distinguish the true from the false?
On the first day of the second month, he ascended the hall and said: "Like this very morning of the first day of the month, the wind and light break through the jade, and the hundred flowers are new.
The Original Patriarch from the West has returned; ten thousand mountains and a thousand peaks are all his kin. At this very moment,"
To call it the meaning of the Patriarch is not permissible; to call it the meaning of the spring scenery is also not permissible.
But tell me, what meaning is it? He raised his whisk and said, "A dot."
Frost said: "The spring flowers remain as they were; ten thousand years are but spring. A fragrant character manifests a fresh blossom.
Clearly at the head of the hundred grasses, vividly lies the intent of the Patriarchs. To call it 'grass' is correct; to call it 'the Patriarch' is also correct.
Yet, that final point remains beyond anyone's comprehension."

In the same small *sǎn* (informal discourse), he said: "The whip steals spring; wild plum blossoms spit forth jade. This single path of the present age is clearly manifest throughout the Manzhou [the world].
Yet, as for this wondrous way beyond kalpas, those who reach it are still rare. Fortunately, you have trodden across this subtle path during the night.
Bring forth your profound mind and come to meet me. If you do not, what kind of 'bowl-dropping ghost' are you?"
The Frost said: "At the beginning, it was used to awaken people to their own functioning amidst the dust and wind of every place.
What was its application? Where did the intent lie? At the very end, it was used to awaken people to the true return to the Buddha-source of all Buddhas.
What was its dynamic function? Where did the intent lie? If, between the past and the present, one can shift this pivot and turn this handle, then the whole world—"
People can do nothing about it. Furthermore, what is this? If it were not so, what kind of "bowl-dropping ghost" would he be?

On the day of the second month’s full moon, the anniversary of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall and said: “The Great Immortal of the land of Chu [India] has today announced his *parinirvāṇa*.”
The rice-son of He-lin attained the "withered" state in an instant. Tell me, is this the same or different?

The body with the characteristics of the four elements is the Tathāgata’s six-foot form; the body without the characteristics of the four elements is the Tathāgata’s single true vision. At that time, people saw extinction.
When the mountain monk saw life, people saw life; when the mountain monk saw death, people saw death. Within this interval lies the principle of neither arising nor ceasing.
Thus, Mahākāśyapa emerged from his coffin with his two feet crossed before Mahābodhi. What is this wondrous inscription of the Mind-Seal?
Fengshuang said: "The Great Sage Śākyamuni never manifested entry into parinirvāṇa; he alone, amidst the grains of rice, took parinirvāṇa as his joy.

This is because the character for 'rice' (米) is composed of the eight characters for 'wood' (木). By means of these eight wooden trees, the Tathāgata clearly illustrates formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
But tell me, what is the matter in between? It is the single point of the wondrous text of the Mind-Seal."
"It cannot be used. Let those who claim they know it put it to the test.
At the same time, he said during a small-scale sermon (xiaocan): "Look, look! The assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemn and has not yet dispersed.
Look, look! The multitude at Jingci are majestic and do not fall into disorder. But tell me, for what reason did the Tathāgata enter the empty cave at that time? Why was this so?"
This mountain monk ascends the empty hall; in the end, he has grown old and frail beyond measure. When you all enter the Nirvana Hall, how will you bring it to mind?
I recall that when Master Xinfeng was at the end of his life, he asked a monk, "Apart from this leaking shell, where shall we meet?
The monk had no reply. Then, sitting upon the empty seat, Master Xinfeng uttered this verse: "Study..."
"Among those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not one has attained awakening. The fault lies in seeking a path on the tip of the tongue.
If you wish to forget form and obliterate all traces, exert yourself with earnest diligence in walking through the void. How does one carry out such instructions? After a long silence, he said, "Ho!
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust [this matter]. He then opened his hands wide and said, "Only thus can one reach the ultimate end."
Frost said: "At the single assembly on Vulture Peak, who was able to see it? The clouds over the Southern Mountain are dense and vast;
among the assembly at Jingci, who knows this? From where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come?
Since I, this old monk, arrived, I could not help but let out a hearty laugh at the very end. Yet, alas, I am forced to expose my family's private flaws before the public. It is truly regrettable.
Jiur said: "Stretching out one's hand—what kind of mental activity is this? Do not take up old sorrows; new sorrows will kill you.
On the first day of the third month, he ascended the hall and said: "The flower-moon today precedes the rising sun; The crescent wheel revolves everywhere across the heavens."
The fragrance of the branch flowers remains rich and pure; the crows and magpies have always shared the night with the moon. To transcend the world: the sun of wisdom shines upon the world.
To proclaim the teaching: he widely opens the gate of ambrosia. Striking his staff once, he said: "The crow's perch is bound layer upon layer;
the patched robe is stitched inch by inch."

Shuang said: "Why compare the bright morning sun to the night moon? For example, the two eyes of every person, the sun and moon in the heavens, and the grasses and trees on earth—all are the functioning of the Dharma King.
Have you not seen it said that the myriad phenomena of the forest and sky are the ancestral style of the Buddhas, and the azure void and clear sky are the livelihood of the Way-man?"
In the same small assembly (small *sǎn*), he said: "The field of wondrous clarity is dense and profound, utterly transcending all opposition and relation.
The workings of the spiritual source are vividly clear, yet free from form and appearance. The functioning of the patch-robed monk is distinct and manifest as his livelihood.
The deluded pursuit of samādhi is vast and bustling, with no end in sight. When, in the end, one is buried in a single pit—where will you find a place to settle your body and establish your life?"
He departed. After a long while, he said: "Ten years have passed without my being able to return; I have forgotten the path by which I came. Fengxue asked:

"What is 'wondrous clarity, clarity that is wondrous,' which not even a thousand sages can carry away? Yangshan replied: "It is the hall where all sages sit. Yangshan asked: "What is 'spiritual continuity, continuity that is spiritual'?

Yangshan replied: "It is the eye for raising the whisk and wielding the mallet. Yangshan asked: "What is the functioning of a patch-robed monk? Yangshan replied: "It is the eye for raising the whisk and wielding the mallet."
What is the samādhi of the deluded path? It is the intention of fine rain and fine sun. Now tell me, what is the matter of burying everything in one pit?
At the river crossing at dusk, the traveler calls for a boat; under the bright sky over the river, people emerge from their houses.
In the end, they still carry this air of elegance with them.
On the fifteenth day of the third month, he ascended the hall and said: "Flowers fall in Qin River Valley; the flowing water is fragrant. The rain clears the jade lotus;
the wondrous pearl is hidden within. Such is the straightforward transmission of this patriarch— To look upon it, not even a single point corresponds.

In the still night, the bell-sound on the tower is cold; The colors of late spring are entrusted to the crimson sun. Most excellent is the solitary loftiness filling the hall— One knows not of the human world."
Upon seeing the golden seal, Chōshō said, "The first two lines are flower-talk that responds to the season. The next two lines do not fall into the trap of that preceding flower-talk.
The final two lines are the sound of a bell in a still night and the colors of a mountain peak in late spring. At such a time, who can understand this? Next...
Although these two lines are lofty and majestic throughout the hall, no one has ever known this scene; they merely chew over the phrasing and recite them.
But tell me, who is it that attains it? At the small public sermon, he said:
"Peaches red, plums white, fallen on the empty steps; The sky azure, the earth green, suspended upon a brocade loom. Clouds and cranes..."

Emerging from the cage and passing through the bird-path; when the profound secret instructions have been fully mastered and no longer transmitted—though one may tread this way, it is not yet the true practice of a monk.
Ultimately, when returning home in poverty, what then? In the wine shops of the human world, the golden terrace meets the evening clouds.
Frost says: Peaches red and plums white fall upon the empty courtyard; Shattering form, they return to emptiness. The azure sky and green earth hang like a brocade loom.
In the moment of the luminous, perfect nature, Clouds and cranes escape their cages as birds pass through the path of the void. The moon sets into the clear pool—emptiness.
When the profound secret instructions have been fully mastered and no longer transmitted, the place of arrival is deep and secluded. But tell me, what is it like when one returns home in poverty?
Emerging from within one’s own station, one wears a straw hat that covers the heavens and sandals that tread upon the earth.
What was thought to be the path for a new year is, in truth, but a dream of a ruined house.
On the first day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall and said: "In other months it was so; today is the first day of the month.

The green trees across the mountains cast their shadows in lush jade; that such strange sprouts flourish so profusely is precisely this. The entire expanse of the great earth cannot be fully captured in a painting.

He recalled an ancient master’s verse on mountain dwelling: "To study the Way, one must first learn poverty; once poverty is learned, the Way will become intimate. In poverty and the Way, there is originally nothing at all."
All things are used in their various ways, yet they are ever new. But tell me, where did the ancients find room for themselves?
You must know that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—they all wear fur and horns. He then raised his whisk and said: "Look, look! What can you call 'extraordinary'?"
Fangshuang said: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the enjoyment of samādhi. From where have you received this news?
Since there is not a single thing, why is everything so new? Since there is nothing extra, why do you say, 'Look'? Therefore it is said:
"Not a single word is spoken, yet the eloquence flows like a hanging river."
In the same small assembly (small *sǎn*), he said: "In the place where the myriad peaks are dense and lush, a cool breeze wafts, washing away the summer heat.
Today, when one’s eyes are truly right, the sharp sword is made of tempered steel. Who says that what is mixed up is deluded attachment? The mountain monk says:
delusive thoughts are the true realm. Thus, the Sūtra says: "At all times, do not give rise to delusive thoughts; yet do not attempt to extinguish these various delusive minds. Abide in delusion..."
When one does not apply further cognitive discernment to the objects of thought, and in the absence of such discernment does not distinguish reality—how then can one tread this path?
After a long silence, he said: "Nature is inherently equal; there is no one who brings about equality."

Fangshuang said: "Our Holy Master traveled through the Five Indias; the Wondrous One opened up the realization and vision of the Single Reality. Thus, he led by the branches and pulled along the vines.
Had he not appeared in the world, who could have unraveled this news? Ultimately, how is it? This Dharma abides in its own station;
the characteristics of the world are eternally constant."

On the occasion of the formal commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in the fourth month, he ascended the hall and said: "Restraining the feet and protecting life amidst the winding and straight paths;
during the retreat, gathering the mind, the faculty is worn smooth. A single incense burner’s fragrance fills the room; the Yellow-Faced Teacher plays with both the clumsy and the clever.
Although it is thus, one must truly reach this stage before it can be attained. Today, let us see how I speak with you all: do not give rise to a single thought of distraction."

"Mindfulness. This is precisely the gathering of mindfulness during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Only when one does not travel upon external paths is it truly the "binding of the feet" (*pādabandhana*) and the protection of life.

Since one no longer travels upon external paths, the heavens, mountains, earth, and valleys are all wondrous realms. When even a single thought does not arise, the mind-consciousness and mental-emotions are entirely within the profound abode.
Even if you were to penetrate this barrier, would that still be sufficient for true joy? Tell me, what do you take to be right? Then he raised his staff.
Raising his sitting mat, he said: "Look! Look! The mountains, rivers, and great earth have transformed into a golden-maned lion and manifested as a jade-tusked elephant king.
Thereupon, he cast down the mat and let out a shout, saying: "By what means is this Dharma-gate established?"
Fangshuang said: "Heaven and earth spread forth auspiciousness; mountains and rivers display their blessings. It does not hinder one’s dwelling in tranquility with feet restrained.
Since a single sitting mat has been transformed into a golden lion and a jade elephant king, it must indeed be extraordinary.
Among these, what was the intent behind that final shout and the casting down of the sitting mat? He uttered the shout: 'What is this?'"
In the same small *sǎn* (informal discourse), he said: "A celestial bridge spans the sea; a stone man runs upon the jade steps.
Who can sing the song of the Mysterious Source? A wondrous singing—how could it be known? Tell me, who shall recognize it?

The iron ox breaks through dreams within the idle fields; the jade horse takes up the whip beyond the Wowa River. From this, the function of the present moment emerges, penetrating everywhere in all directions.
It is clear. Changshou said: "A celestial bridge spans across the sea; it is a bridge that connects antiquity with the present. A stone man runs up the jade steps;
this is the mechanism for entering directly into the truth. Who can sing the song of the profound source? To whom can one speak the news from within this station? It is wondrous.
How could one know by chanting "Qi"? Only at the depths of the clear pool can one see the fish.
But tell me, who will recognize this? Beside it, the horns and fur are perfectly complete. When the Iron Ox shatters the dream, it plows through the fields of empty kalpas.
When the Jade Horse takes up the whip, it gallops across the Manzhou Wob. When there is penetration in all seven directions and eight ways, only then is it truly everywhere.
It is clear: that which is there is the same as that which is here; this and that are blended and fused, and one attains the wondrous at every moment.
But tell me, in whose sphere does this lie?

On the first day of the fifth month, he ascended the hall and said: "The first light of the morning sun upon this day of the *gao* month; its jade brilliance pierces the darkness, revealing its majestic presence.
Day after day, the events of the distant past are made clear: that auspicious time beyond the limit of *Vibhūṣaṇa* (Weiyin).

Sometimes one goes beneath the ten-thousand-year-old pines beyond the heavens; sometimes one comes amidst the clouds upon the rivers of a thousand ages; sometimes one abides fragrantly within the dust."
Turning around, he may stride with poised majesty within the light; ultimately, throughout the heavens above and the earth below, there is nowhere this samādhi does not reach.
Tell me, by whose power of grace is this achieved?
Fangshuang said: "Sometimes one contemplates that vast antiquity as if it were this very day; sometimes the entire body and all its reaches vanish, and the whole being forgets its nature.
Then, one arrives at the dimly visible steps by the Reed River at dusk, appearing as if emerging from the mechanisms of the ancient peaks."
One must know that throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, one is entirely sustained by the support of others, yet one’s own power is fully revealed.
As stated in the *Xiaocan*: "The plum rains at Mount Gu fall in steady torrents; ripe fruit falls to the ground; the cuckoo cries upon the branches."
A cool breeze blows and the crystal curtain stirs. This mountain monk addresses the assembly with these idle words; how can you practitioners hear them?
If you try to see and hear them with your ears, it will ultimately be difficult to speak of them. If you attempt to fathom them through speech and thought, you only humiliate yourself.
But tell me, why is this so? Even the Yellow-Faced Gautama or the Blue-Eyed Barbarian monks would find it difficult to discern.
"Let those with eyes look for themselves.
Shuang said, "Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was already this news. Before the Patriarch came from the West, there has been a wondrous secret from of old.
Even before the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared, there was still a wondrous meaning; how much more so after they have arisen?"
"Is it that you have failed to grasp what has come? Furthermore, tell me, what principle is this? This is a ready-made koan; it is most difficult, most difficult.

On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, Chan Master Banxian ascended the hall and said: "Behold, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, the mountain peaks are covered with snowflakes falling to the ground."
Soaring: Last night the black bird entered beyond the clouds; this morning the egret and crane emerge from the Purple Microcosm. The wooden horse neighs repeatedly in the north wind;

the golden goose cries out with every mouth at the southern branch. The stone old man’s spirit is emaciated and his stride is severed; the jade youth’s sentiment is abundant and his fists are rarely raised.
Fangshuang said: "If a master of the house does not possess such eyes, how can he discern the true source of the wind from afar?
He must employ a mechanism beyond the ordinary to respond to one who stands outside of all things. I, this poor monk, have added these footnotes; it already constitutes a matter of profit and loss.
But ultimately, what of it? Riding a tiger through the marketplace; holding a torch to steal a pig."
In the same small assembly, he said: "Today the mountain monk has spoken eight lines of verse.
How does each of you understand them? Tonight I cannot help but add further humble words. Tell me, are they the same as today, or are they different?
He took up his staff, threw it down before the steps, and said: "The other family has its own path to the heavens; why laboriously seek another way? Wei.
"From the towering summit, it falls to the bottom of the pool; the sharp, austere family style blows along the road. These are four lines of verse.
The assembly in the hall each requested the subsequent lines, saying, "If you do not provide them, we shall return to the hall to sleep."
Fangshuang said: "Using morning attendance and evening requests—why? Every word hits the mark; there is nothing beyond this.
Nevertheless, it is like adding mud to earth or pearls to jade. Casually, I shall provide four lines to continue the Master’s rhyme.
How do you all fare? An eight-foot black staff beyond heaven and earth; a thousand-fathom fishing line, the path for catching fish. Orthodoxy and Deviation."
Reciprocity is also not required; the wild flute blows into the path of the woodcutter.
On the day of the midsummer retreat in the sixth month, he ascended the hall and said: "Today is the midsummer season;
for those who practice the Way, there is neither distance nor intimacy. In the light, the guest contains the host; in the dark, the host contains the guest. Dark within the dark, yet not—"
The clarity within the state is true; it is luminous and luminous, never dark, before the eyes of people. Yet, what is there ultimately to grasp? Look, look at that solitary, towering unicorn.
Remember how the ancient Buddha Hongzhi ascended the seat and said: "The wondrous exists in profound stillness, yet is not 'existent';
the true illumination is spiritually alert, yet is not 'non-existent. Furthermore, within this very midst, step back and look—where the white clouds are severed."
Abiding amidst the green mountains, how can you all carry such baggage? True merit in quiescence has no substance;

the wondrous principle of non-merit is profoundly deep. Within sameness there is difference, within the coarse there is the subtle; within difference there is sameness, within thought there is the mind.
Frost said: "The passage of time is to be cherished; days and months fly like arrows. Do not forget this single thought for a moment. The Buddhas and Patriarchs are like a flowing stream;
the sages are distant, while the times of calamity flourish. You must clarify this matter. The Buddha-dharma has no divergent paths; it simply follows where people excel.
Those of superior faculties and wondrous capacity awaken and turn about in a single stroke, casting off every word as they speak."
Regarding these supreme and wondrous phrases: those of medium capacity and keen faculties distinguish the coarse within the subtle and discern the coarse within the subtle;
they unite father and mother to form the mouth of birth, opening the gate of proclamation shown by the thousand sages.

For those of inferior capacity and ordinary inclinations, they recognize the sage within the mundane and withdraw the mind into the depths of thought; single-mindedly kneeling, they exhaust all delusions from time to time, ultimately attaining realization.
And what thing is it? Look, look at this solitary, towering unicorn.
In the same small *sīmān* (private instruction), he said: "At night, washing away the heat, a cool breeze drifts; in the sixth month, bright and clear, the heavens are filled with snow.

When the green groves grow dim at evening, people return to their homes; when the red valleys break into light at dawn, travelers call out for the moon. A single speck of dust enters into right concentration (*samādhi*), shining brilliantly white.
Within the Samādhi of Illusion, the various dharmas of samādhi arise; one clearly perceives the workings of the Samādhi of the Emanation Body.
The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and the myriad billions of wondrous meanings—take them up and look at them as a single spark.
If you cannot discern them all, you are merely a fellow who tears up his own mats in vain.
Sōng said: "The first two lines illustrate the state of the Dharmakāya. The next line is the model for reaching the secret place.
The final line is the conclusion. Furthermore, returning to the midway lodging at Rubang is called 'entering the Illusory Samādhi.
From this point on, following along until every matter is unimpeded is called 'attaining the Nirmāṇakāya.'"
The matter of samādhi. Tell me, what is it that attains such freedom? Speak for me!
If you cannot, you are merely a fellow who tears up his shop to make a temporary pretext for tea-talk. As for hearing: "The drifting clouds emerge from the peaks;
the clear moon washes the mountain stream."
On the third day of the fifth month, he ascended the hall and said: "The jade mechanism turns; the golden hall grows cold. The stone chamber opens askew; the iron door shines bright.
The wooden cock calls the moon as the jar-heaven dawns; the clay ox roars amidst the flowers as the guest wanders the city. At this very moment—"
The green mountains are mindless, neighbors to the white clouds; the white horse, without a whip, emerges from the reeds. The path is not the old way; the person does not forget their home.
With solemn dignity, they return and immediately become a water buffalo. Its horns and hair are stubborn and coarse; it plows the fields by the river.
The Plow. At the foot of the mountain, the plowing has ceased; one must know that the true place for the conduct of a śramaṇa is here.
Only then will one follow types without falling into them and follow forms without being obstructed by them. Monks of the present day should investigate in this manner.
Shuang said: "The first 'down' lands within a single *gongwei*; having attained the subtle, one merely turns the body.
The second 'down' acts as a noseless needle crossing the line from here; midway, the pivot has not yet been grasped.

The third turn of the sublime purport again touches upon the clarity of heaven, yet it still reports to the barbarian. The fourth, the patterned dark phrase, takes lodging at Lujiang; furthermore, it shatters the dream of the leaking raft."
For a moment, one attains a slight resonance of voice and countenance; this arises from the bottom of the profound source’s lucid illumination.

It is able to emit light and manifest responses, such that all various sensory objects appear vividly and clearly without omission. If you can realize and carry this understanding in this way, you will succeed.
"The house to the east makes a horse; the house to the west makes a donkey—this is no hindrance. But tell me, in whose sphere does this lie? He then gave a small public discourse, saying:
"The place where all Buddhas emerge is where the mountain flows upon the water. In the imperial palace, jade curtains hang down; in the cloud-chamber, the heavens are embraced in azure.
The white snows of the three winters and the green trees of the nine summers; seeing fresh cool water, one’s joy increases anew."
In the cold and ice, one dwells in the summer retreat with the assembly; restraining the feet to protect living beings, arriving early and departing late.
If you understand this message, you may traverse the world at will, your feet treading solid ground. If it is not yet so, you are merely a man wandering from east to west.
Shuang said: "The five Mount Sumerus, the two Iron Ring Peaks, the Great Garuda soaring through the nine heavens, and the flying dragon leaping beyond the seas—these are remembered.
A monk once asked Yunmen, 'What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen replied, 'On the water above the East Mountain.
The monk asked, 'How can one understand this? Yunmen gave him a punch and said, 'What is this? This is a direct interception."
Question: This response given in reply to the question is like a father and mother hanging out their tongues; how, after all, should one practice and tread upon it?
I, this poor monk, shall suddenly utter four lines of verse for you. Is this correct or biased? Let those among the assembly who possess the "extra horn" try to judge it.
On the seventh day of the seventh month, he ascended the hall and said: "The moon’s appearance today is bright with the morning sun; a single leaf of the paulownia tree falls in the golden wind.
The autumn sounds are desolate, like yellow jade; atop the mountain, the heavens are filled with sorrow. The functional application before one’s eyes has nothing beyond it;
where else could there be a wondrous verse that transcends myriad efforts? The soul of the dreaming butterfly flies into the great void; the fisherman who lost his boat [returns]."
Mooring my solitary sail, Hu Wenxin sends me a northern wild goose. Only now do I see the message from home; its merit shall be realized on another day.
After the mountains have turned and the moon becomes bright, the road back home stretches long and clear, shimmering like jade.
Shuang said: "In general, the first four lines clarify the functioning of the present moment; the next four lines clarify the winding and lateral engagement within the stages.

The Village Road. Before the Great Compassion Hall is Dingzhou; before the Yellow Crane Tower is Yingwu Isle. Descending from his seat, he said:

Fangshuang said: "The first four lines describe not emerging from within the world-transcending;

Therefore, Dongshan said: "Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, the nine months of summer pass by at every moment. Tell me, when it comes—when it comes—how is it?
Internally and externally empty and vast, the Dharma-realm is as one. Thus it is said: "Sitting, reclining, and walking in the Pūrvavideha continent—this is the mark of such a Great Man."

In the same informal discourse (small *sǎn*), he said: "The air beyond the heavens is cold; the ancestral style is naturally austere. When the green mountains take a step, the stone woman gives birth to a child;

Beyond the balustrade, the foliage is lush and dense, and the fragrant grove lies there; atop the ridge, the scene is desolate and cool, yet the moon is perfectly clear.
This is a fine occasion. Do you all understand? It is able to act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, never withering throughout the four seasons.

Frost said: "The air beyond the heavens is cold, and the family style is naturally withered. Only when one is personally enlightened does the mountain green move its steps and the stone woman give birth to a child.
When the primordial chaos gives rise to the One Qi and turns its function inward, the wooden man returns the breath and the iron man shatters his dreams.
As the moon’s shadow shifts its light, the sun’s orb emits its brilliance; they come together, and there is no hindrance."

Thus it has come to pass that you still have breath remaining. This is precisely the time for drinking tea and chatting in laughter.
On an auspicious day in the eighth month, he ascended the hall and said: "Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, there was already this wondrous Dharma;

Do you understand? "Luminous jade is without flaw; carved patterns destroy virtue.
He said in a small *can*: "In the mid-autumn moon, pearls are born at the River of Conch Shells; when the grasses are lush with dew, the shadow-hare conceives."
Suddenly, if a man were to come forth and ask, "By what means shall you test me?"—whether with a staff or a shout; whether with a second or third phrase, or with words and speech;

whether through the seven perversions; whether by brandishing a staff or holding up a whisk, or by mimicking gestures and postures; or by joining the ten fingers, bowing the body, and performing ritual prostrations.

Furthermore, tell me: by what means can this be discerned? When questioned, one answers immediately; opening their mouth reveals their very heart. Penetrating in eight ways and reaching in nine, they do not expose even the tip of a needle.
Shuang said: "Water is tested with a staff; jade is tested with fire; the human world is verified through speech; and Chan monks are [verified] by..."
How is this verified? He struck the meditation platform and said, "Take care during the night.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, he ascended the hall and said: "In this month of autumn, today the half-moon is bright. The eyes of the monks who have come above are wide open;
it is difficult to deceive the diseased eyes of the assembly. What need is there for the sentiments of a son of the Dongshan house? Even so, who [is it]?"
"This is a living eye. Try opening both eyes for this old monk and see. If not, what use is it?
Fang said, "Students of Zen who strive for enlightenment are as numerous as hemp and millet, gathered in crowds and throngs.

It goes down. Nevertheless, though it is so, dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; a patch-robed monk is not easily deceived.
The mind is like ice and snow, its cold penetrating to the very marrow of the bones. If it were otherwise, what would be its function?
In the same small assembly, he said: "The pure lineage of the family is clear in every word, vast and free; the jade bag and golden needle are penetrating in every stroke.
Tonight, with one full moon, a thousand mountains and ten thousand streams flow on; unaware of the iron cauldron of kalpas, it stands majestic, beyond coming or going."
At this very moment, one attains the right and attains the wrong; one attains both the good and the bad, as well as acceptance and rejection. Ultimately, how is it?
After a long silence, he said: "Where the water and sky blend together, ten thousand miles are one with the autumn."
Shuang said: "The 'transmission of a family's purity' refers, it seems, to the 'Snow Song. A monk asked Xinfeng, 'What is the Snow Song?
Feng replied, 'The state of being ten times pure and white. This is because when one does not strive in chanting, every word is expansive and liberated;
this is the meaning of praising the wondrous words of the former master. The jade bag and golden needle—every point is thoroughly penetrated. These four [lines].
These lines are simply the single color of great function. Tonight, a single orb of moon flows through a thousand mountains and ten thousand streams;
unaware of it, the iron cauldron of the kalpa is submerged, leaving nothing behind or before. These four lines are the single color prior to the position of correctness.
At this very moment, rightness and wrongness, good and evil, acceptance and rejection—all are attained. These four lines are the single color of the present time.
Indeed. Ultimately, when the three colors are all attained, they are like water and sky blending together, where ten thousand miles are unified in autumn.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, he ascended the hall and said: "The profound month is today, the season of white chrysanthemums; The heavenly grass containing pearls has not yet opened its gold.

What is the purpose of speaking in advance to the great assembly on the Double Ninth? If you reach the ninth day, do not say that I have not said it.
Countless Bodhisattvas come; here, this old monk opens immeasurable Dharma gates. People of the time call this the "Chrysanthemum Samādhi"—thirty blows!
To call it "countless Bodhisattvas" is another thirty blows! Only then will I allow you to carry it away.

"From where does this fundamental substance come? It is something beyond the ordinary. He gave a shout and said, "It comes straight down; look quickly with your eyes!

He was born only to follow people into goodness. Wan struck him once with his fist and said, "Even though your eyebrows have been burned away, you still do not know.
The monk made a gesture of fear. This monk, with a single hearth-fire deity, sought to burn Master Wan’s face; Wan secretly rinsed his mouth with water to ward off the fire.

If you allow for any deliberation or hesitation, there will be ten thousand miles of white clouds. He then spread both palms, stroked them, and said: "Jian!"

This assembly of Chan companions has entered the formal retreat for three lifetimes. Time is to be cherished, yet the flowers of the year do not linger. From dawn until dusk, we eat our meals and drink our tea.
Among these practitioners, there is not one who possesses a true Chan mind. From birth until old age, these seekers of the Way have merely donned robes and engaged in idle chatter."
"If you do not know your own mind, your mental recitations are but a weary labor; you fail to recognize the profound essence. How bitter and tragic! This poor monk is solitary and aged;
my years are spent and difficult to restrain. I earnestly exhort the assembly of monks to place your lifelong trust in this.
He then threw down his staff and said, "Look! Look! He spoke again: "What skillful means does this old monk possess?"

where does the meaning lie? He suddenly struck the meditation seat and said, "Look! Look! What skill do you have?"

When the drum is beaten in the Great Tang, the people of Silla break into dance."
Shuang said: "The horse in Qizhou eats rice; the ox in Fuzhou has a full belly. This line of discourse possesses a mechanism beyond the ordinary;
it may be said to possess a strategy that transcends all things.
On the first day of the eleventh month, he ascended the hall and said: "The first day of this month of Ku; it is precisely the winter solstice, when the frosty moon is full.
This auspicious festival of the first yang—everyone, look at these characters! Every word contains the profound mystery as they face the bright sun.
Spreading out both hands, he said: "The rocks roll and the sand flies!"
Frost said: "It is precisely today, the festival of the first yang. On the winter solstice, the wind and light wipe away the snowy moon;
the frost-blade and sword-gas sever the ten thousand heavens. This is a fine season for the human world. Within this, what kind of literary composition is it to extend both hands?
Following that, to say 'stones run and sand flies'—what kind of flowery talk is that? It is adding frost to snow."
In the same small session, he said: "The wind blows through the pines and snow; the moon is in the sky. Within the function of this single color, one turns their steps together.

Frost said: "The season is cold and frigid; the pines and cypresses are steep and lofty. Where everything is rendered in a single color, the ten thousand mountains are a landscape of cold.

To discern the wondrous place apart from this—to make the word 'different' clear—is when one color transforms into another color, and true function accords with true function. This is not due to matters of today."

Furthermore, they contend that Master Zuo Xuwen’s lecture on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month stated: "The green mountains are dense and secluded, yet the traveler finds it difficult to reach this place;

South Mountain is verdant and its waterways flow far; North Creek is silent and its icy bones are cold.

In the same small assembly (small *sǎn*), he said: "The luster of the uncut jade is as cold as the air of ice and snow; The integrity of the pine and cypress is revealed within the clear water.

In the celestial palace of Śakra, the jeweled nets are layered upon one another; beneath the lion throne of Śākyamuni, the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) is majestic and vast.

The realm of Mañjuśrī is where Samantabhadra sits; the realm of Samantabhadra is where Mañjuśrī sits. When one reaches this point, it is the state of the Sage.

He gave a small-scale discourse (xiao can), saying: "In a cold night without charcoal, the old man’s robes are thin; The cool wind penetrates the bones as the ancient hall is dim.

The Frost said: "Clothes are thin and the cold penetrates my iron bones; my body is worn out and I am weary of explaining all these matters.

On the night of the full moon in the twelfth month, he ascended the hall and said: "The northern face has half its window shrouded in deep shadow; The southern side has its entire room bathed in slanting sunlight.
This has nothing to do with the influence of yin or the brilliance of yang; Upon the ridge, the snow is so cold that white appears as black."
Frost said: "North and south, yin and yang, the branches of the lineage and the roots of Chan, guest and host awaiting one another—without crossing over these two places, where would you go?
The heavens above the four quarters take the celestial realms as their limit; the three realms take the formless realm as their limit;
the human world takes a hundred years as its limit; the four seasons take the winter snows as their limit. Is this not merely clinging to limits?"
Furthermore, tell me: why is the snow on the mountain peak white yet appears black? Please try to discern this. In the same small *sāṃkathya* (informal discourse), he said:
"The sky is cold and the plum blossoms are constrained; the earth is frigid and the fish are submerged in water.
Therefore it is said: when it is cold, heaven and earth are cold throughout; when it is hot, heaven and earth are hot throughout. Now tell me, where does one descend [into realization]?

The Master then said, "The essential point of study and awakening must be the essential point of reaching true realization. On the path of Zen practice, one must also achieve wondrous resonance."
The path of each is to request that half a seat be shared; then, descend from the seat.
Shuang said: "To discuss right and wrong with an eye that penetrates both ancient and modern is not as good as the Subtle [Dharma]. Tell me, by what cause is this attained?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single ray of grace is difficult to repay for ten thousand years; a thousand words of learned speech are easily heard throughout three lifetimes.
When one is precisely at this point, how does one pivot? At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Master, you must be seeking some underlying trace."
The Master struck him and said, "Tell me, what season is this? At these words, the monk suddenly attained great enlightenment.
The Master then said, "For eleven years I have proclaimed the profound and manifested the shallow; today at last I have met one who understands my music. May a thousand blessings multiply! Why?
For three years I cast my fishing line, and in a single night I caught the golden-scaled fish. He then descended from his seat.

Shuang said: "Ripe fruit cannot remain upon the branch; the radiance of a sword does not obstruct the heavens. This monk knows the sensation of pain and itch; the old monk distinguishes the appropriate occasion.

He ascended the hall and said: "Withered trees are shrouded in elegant clouds; within the clouds, jade-like figures stand tall. In the cold pond, the moon is full at night; at the bottom of the pond..."
The fish invades and enters; turning his head, he opens the true eye. Wearing a cap upon his head, he emerges; fragrant grass breaks through the spring mist.
The lush green grass brushes against the heavens—can anyone among you speak of this? At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and asked, "What do all the sages come forth to do?
The Master said, "It is because you do not understand how to take it up. The monk said, "What a wonderful message! I have never understood it before."

[The monk] took [the staff]. The Master said, "I knew early on where you would land. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Wrong. The Master then said, "If you understand this, you are Kāśyapa of Vulture Peak;
if you do not understand it, you are Huike of Shaolin. Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
Shuang said: "At Vulture Peak, the smile is warm; at Shaolin, the seat is cold. A single flower before the kalpas—spring outside the gate remains locked.
He ascended the hall and said: "The green cliffs and withered trees do not fall into the human realm; the fragrant grasses of the red valleys neither loathe warmth nor cold. To the west..."
South, north, east, and west—each is unrelated. At this profound point of the three sections, look directly with your own eyes.

At that time, a monk came forth from the assembly and asked, "What is the green cliff and the withered tree? The Master said, "The axe cannot cleave it open. The monk asked, "What is the red valley and the fragrant grass?
The Master said, "The iron spear cannot mow them down. "How can they be mowed down? the monk asked. "Southwest, east," the Master replied.

"What is the purpose of 'the North'? The Master said, "Before one's eyes, it does not interfere with anything extra. The Master then said: "The ground of wondrous profundity can be reached by oneself;
the place where the numinous nature acts can be sat upon by oneself; the clear and distinct timing can be seen by oneself.
One must strive for this; it cannot be realized by questioning others. Once you have personally penetrated to the very summit, then descend from the seat."
Shuang said: "Sometimes high, sometimes low; sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest. Ultimately, there must be the illumination of self-reflection.
Even so, one must truly reach this state before it can be attained."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The full moon emerges with its coolness; the bright sun enters with its warmth. The light of wisdom breaks through darkness; as soon as it shines, all is illuminated. Within this, there is one Buddha appearing in the world.

If anyone can perceive this, they will realize that it is not merely their own 'wondrous existence,' yet they will also know that the pervasive light extends throughout the sands of the Buddha-worlds.
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked: "Setting aside for a moment this wondrous existence and pervasive light, what is this 'one Buddha'?"

The Master said, "It illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction. The monk asked, "If that is so, then the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena above heaven and below earth [is revealed].
The Master said, "How is it that you possess the wisdom of Nāgārjuna? The monk said, "How is it that you possess the marvelous talent of Aśvaghoṣa?
The Master said, "Even so, do you not still fail to distinguish [the two]? The monk then bowed and departed. As the Master saw him off, he said:
He had observed dietary restrictions for thirty years. The Master then said, "The mark of the invisible crown of the head is unknown to ordinary people;

the wondrous light of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra shines universally throughout the sands of the Ganges. Therefore it is said that the World-Honored One’s light struck Ānanda’s shoulder. He then descended from his seat.
Fangshuang said: "The morning sun, the evening glow, the first moon, and the fading light—these realms before one's eyes can still be observed.
But as for that azure within the eye, who dares to see it? To open the true eye, one must be a person with a living mind."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Every step taken is majestic; the entire body is vividly present. Speaking eastward and westward, coming from the south and going to the north, one fully possesses the inch-sized mind and directly employs the foot-measure of sentiment.
He took up his staff and said, "The Lord of the Master’s own heart has now become this wooden monk in my palm.
He then raised his whisk and said, "For eighty years, I have sought to rectify what is held in the hand."
"Elder Hào, let those with eyes look! At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, 'Ultimately, how far apart are they?
The Master said, 'This is a matter for you, a student. The monk asked, 'And what is it for the Master? The Master stood with his hands folded in a state of profound stillness.
The Master then said, 'Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, one is entirely sustained by his grace and power. [He then inquired after the Master's] health.
"The substance of stillness and motion being as one. He then descended from his seat.
Shuang said, "The moon in the heavens finds it easy to rest upon the water; the wild geese from the north find it difficult to lodge without the forest."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The site of the ancient Buddhas’ enlightenment still requires one to ride in a carriage; the waters of the deep source pool still require one to row a fox-boat. The night crane pierces the bottom of the pool;
the clouds and moon fall into a silver cage. The celestial dragons bring no rain; the sweating horses have no whips. From this, the calf-bull is born;
its golden roars and silver cries fill the reed waters. Its fine hairs remain, as ever, in the state of right reception."
In the midst [of this], the dark horn again bears drifting snow and weeds. Once, riding backward like a shepherd boy in a dream, he plays several flutes as a woodcutter’s song comes drifting in.
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Ultimately, how should a student deliberate upon this?
The Master said, "To penetrate to the very top and through to the bottom, one must understand it thus. The monk then bowed, and the Master said, "This is the kind of grass grown in my own house."
The Master then said, "For those who seek fabricated fabrications, not a single word of profound discourse or wondrous phrasing will suffice;
not a speck of golden words or flowery language shall be used. Please try to speak for me. He then descended from his seat.
Fangshuang said: "The site of the ancient Buddhas' practice does not require sitting. When the night cranes, clouds, and moon pass through until they have fallen away;

when the dragon’s sweat-horses and the rain-stopping whips are gone—within this realm beyond the mundane, who dares to deliberate? This is simply because those with the subtle essence rarely attain the pivot.
Furthermore, when returning to the fundamental path, the calf born from the ox has its hair and horns complete. Even so, it is not yet [the end]."
This is plowing and breaking through a field of land; one must awaken from half-dreaming. Furthermore, one blows the mad flute;
at that moment, the hooves tread everywhere through the muddy dust, yet the true mechanism is not revealed. Tell me, this is still a matter on the side of transcending the world.
But when it comes to the time of not yet having transcended the world, how is it? The weeds of our own house do not seek out arbitrary fabrications.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The great matter of traveling on pilgrimage and the essential point of our school consist simply in picking up the Buddha-staff made of rabbit horns and holding aloft the patriarchal whisk made of tortoise hair.
If anyone were to pick it up and hold it aloft, everyone present would surely offer their thanks.

At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked: "In this assembly within the hall, all are indeed travelers on pilgrimage; yet they have not yet seen the rabbit-horn staff or the tortoise-hair whisk."
Mao, I request that the Master grant me an instruction. The Master cast down his staff and whisk and said, "To see it and not grasp it—this is difficult to encounter in a thousand years.
As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted, "Go on! The Master then said: "When it comes, dragons and snakes fly forth; when it goes, elephants and tigers roar.
To perceive the profound color and wondrous sound, or to engage in calculation and conceptualization regarding the true measure, is why it is said: 'Beyond the like.'"
There is no ignorance. Outside of wisdom, there is no suchness (*tathatā*). Suchness is luminously pure; wisdom is pure. This is, in general, nothing other than the mind of *prajñā*.
Then, he descended from his seat.
Fengshuang said: "Emptiness upon emptiness is suchness; profound stillness is true reality. Yellow chrysanthemums are prajñā;
green bamboo is tathatā. Kāśyapa transmitted it secretly; Ānanda possessed correct knowledge. Vimalakīrti remained silent; Mañjuśrī could hear it."
Ultimately, what kind of power is this? Those who study [the Way] lack these eyes; how then can they distinguish black from white? He ascended the hall and said:
"Mind after mind penetrates through, and phenomenon after phenomenon is perfectly realized. Buddha after Buddha transmits it to one another, and Patriarch after Patriarch hands it down.
Amidst the assembly of monks, while sipping tea, is there anyone who can truly believe this? At that time, there was a monk...

A monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Since this is the state where the mind-dharma is universally perfect and complete, it is precisely the moment when Buddhas and Patriarchs transmit the Dharma.
Apart from this, what else could be called 'external' (non-Buddhist)? The Master said, "This very principle is what constitutes the external.

The monk asked, "What is it like when there is no principle? The Master laughed heartily and said, "Alas! Even this principle is [the external]. The Master then said, "The ripples of the silver river."
The night is clear; the morning stars fly in disorder as the light of the sun’s palace grows cold. The evening chill wipes away the mist, and a faint breeze stirs the reeds outside the railing.

The jade-tree branches move as the stream flows before the balustrade. For an old monk to speak in such a manner—what manner of spirit or eloquence is there? Having said this, he descended from his seat.

Fengshuang said: "I, a poor monk, am unable to offer praise. Why is it so? When it is precisely correct, that very correctness is partial; when it is precisely partial, that very partiality is correct.
Correctness and partiality are harmoniously fused, responding universally to both the high and the low. Have you ultimately exhausted this principle?
On the riverbank, the wind and waves darken at dusk; in the reed village, the scenery is still."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Profoundly deep, one enters the melody of the plum blossoms; subtly hidden, one contains the tune of the falling snow.
The dancing sleeves of the stone man, the flute and song of the jade maidens—what a magnificent musical performance! What kind of resonance is this?"
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "A single-stringed lute—how rare it is for a master hand to play it!
The Master said, "Tell me, whose melody is this? The monk replied, "Fortunately, the Main Peak nods its head and the Foreground Peak turns its gaze back."
The Master said, "From the very beginning, you have been like this for a mere trifle. He then said: "Flowing water plays a tune on a stringless lute;
the night sky strums a melody on a jade zither. An iron man laughs at the stalks of fragrant grass; a stone man sighs over a dream of spring mist.
Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Fangzhongzi said: "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! The dew-pillar preaches the Dharma and the lantern listens. He ascended the hall and said:
"The subtle and profound song—how could it be conveyed by the mark of the tongue? The majestic and true chant—how could it be expressed by sound?
After the dream has awakened for the thousand-year-old crane, a young monk sings the conclusion; the scenery of both courtyards is complete."
"How is it, after all? At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What is the scenery over there?
The Master said, "The green mountains rise high, their traces veiled by cloud-robes. The monk asked, "What is the scenery on this side? The Master said, "Flowing water goes far;
flowing water transforms into waves. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "Dew on the flowers remains as fragrant as in the springtime."
For over a month, the bottom of the pond has held ten-thousand-year light. The Master then said: "The course of the water is cold and chilling;
the form of the clouds is a vast, empty curtain. He then descended from his seat.
Frost said: "The patch-robed monk is of one and the same nature. He plays with the lofty, deep azure heavens and employs the low, shallow crimson steps.
Body and function, partiality and correctness, are all newly manifested at once."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring dream is hazy; the autumn moon is clear and bright. Summer is cool and still; winter is cold and empty.
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "If you do not change throughout the four seasons, what is it? The Master said, "Do you hear me?
The monk said, "Pointing to the house behind, one calls out to the steps before; calling for the white ape to beat the black dog. The Master said, "But I do not permit outsiders to hear this."
The Master then said: "In my school, there is a time of mutual accommodation and a time of non-accommodation;

in my house, there is the manner of transcending the world and the manner of not transcending the world. When there is mutual accommodation, one must not see mutual accommodation; when there is transcendence, one must not see transcendence.
Where does the meaning lie? Where are the eyes? Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Shuang said: "To the east and west of Xi, to the north and south of Hu, he then raised his fist and asked: 'What kind of news is this?
When there is mutual interplay, the intent lies in non-interplay; when one appears in the world, the eye is upon non-appearance."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Emperor of the Liang land and the Crown Prince of Southern Heaven meet face-to-face, yet they do not recognize the wondrous intent.
They do not enter directly; they hesitate and deliberate. Suddenly, all is vast and open—there is no sage.

At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and asked, "Facing one another without private bias, how is it that you do not recognize? The Master struck him and said, "What a fine report! If you hear it, you hear it."
The monk said, "When the great function manifests, no rules or regulations exist. The Master said, "The Third Patriarch has arrived. The Master then said:

"Vast and empty, one does not even recognize whether it is public or private; when the Crown Prince and the Emperor face each other, there is but a single piece of sandalwood incense burning upon the brazier."
"Residual red petals are blown up, causing the flower branches to bloom. He then descended from his seat.

Changshui said, "From the seven Buddhas of antiquity down to the various sages who appeared, from the forty-two patriarchs of the Western Heaven to the two or three masters of this land—how, ultimately, can one recognize them when they arrive at this point? He added, "A dot."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The blade of the divine sword shines within its scabbard; the pure light it illuminates penetrates empty space.

This secret transmission of news is not conveyed through words; its merit differs from that of heaven and earth. At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "I do not know what chapter or verse this refers to.
The Master said, "If you can speak it, then you will understand. The monk asked, "Does the Master know it? The Master said:
"You are a seeker of Chan," the Master said. "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true. He then descended from his seat.
Fang said: "Every word contains the wondrous; every phrase strikes the truth. A fierce tiger emerging from the forest, a dark dragon entering the water—this is right, this is acceptable;
that is not right, that is not acceptable."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes one breaks through the barrier and knows the point of descent; sometimes one penetrates the barrier and discerns the secret purport.

Sometimes it is within the posture of the wondrous countenance; sometimes it is the light illuminating the tip of the pivot. Within this there are essence and function, guest and host; within this there is the winding path of indirect inquiry.
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What is the eye that breaks through the barrier? The Master then—
[The Master] struck him. The monk asked, "What is the point of this? The Master said, "The moon over the reeds and the waves on the river reflect each other in red.
The monk asked, "How can one deliberate upon the pivot that penetrates the barrier? The Master then gave a shout. The monk asked, "What is the secret intent?
The Master said, "Ruler and minister accord with the Way; host and guest are one. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "A thousand waves upon the waters of the long river."
He ran off. By the valley stream, ten thousand clusters of grass grew. The Master then said, "Speaking in the morning and speaking in the evening—this is the extension of the broad and long tongue.
Sitting, reclining, or walking—this is ten thousand miles of tempered steel. He took up his staff and asked, "What is this? Then he descended from his seat.
Shuang said: "True hearing and true seeing; wondrously reaching and wondrously arriving; profound contemplation and profound measure; hidden and manifest.
Although it is thus, one reaches it oneself through thorough penetration."

Ascending the hall, he said: "If you go forward into the state of realization, the cloud-robed traces vanish and the mountains are empty. If you return to the point of the pivot, fire washes the jade path clear.
If there is neither going nor coming, the stone serpent lies coiled in the lush thickets. Ultimately, if one attains thorough understanding, heaven and sea are universally one.
Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had arisen, the news was difficult to transmit. Before humans and devas had recognized it, the wondrous place was without [name]."
Exhausted! Even if it were so, it would certainly not suffice. For now, let us reach this point; do not point toward the east or the west.
At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and asked, "What is the eye that moves forward? The Master said, "Entering straight into the sea, the mud ox leaves no trace."
The monk asked, "What is the eye that comes back? The Master said, "Long ago, before the stall, the jade horse neighed in the wind.
The monk asked, "What is the eye that neither goes nor comes? The Master said, "Sitting alone on a cloud-throne, dwelling of one's own accord in the great void.
The monk asked, "Ultimately, when there is total penetration and understanding, what then? The Master said, "For three years, amidst the golden-haired lions, he was utterly peerless."
The monk asked, "Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had arisen, who was it that attained liberation? The Master said, "The sun rises over the green trees; the moon falls into the water.
The monk asked, "When neither humans nor devas have yet recognized it, tell me, what do you take to be right? The Master said, "A fish moves through a wine shop, coming and going without end.
The monk said, "There is no need for preceding words or following phrases. The Master gave a shout and said, "Turning iron into gold. "Transformation!"

A snake becomes a dragon. The monk said, "I have received your instructions one by one; how is it with the mysterious mechanism beyond the norm? The Master said, "The moon emerges from within the lines;
flowers enter into the midst of the verse. The Master then said: "This single great matter is difficult to penetrate throughout antiquity and the present.

The indirect teachings of the Three Vehicles make coming and going easy to empty. The eyes of a patch-robed monk are truly without artifice; when a Chan practitioner trusts in this, they are liberated."
"Traces are cut off. Although it is thus, only by realizing it can one reach the ultimate exhaustion.
He then descended from his seat. Shuang said, "Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality; for three years, he has been peerless among the flock of golden-haired lions.
That person, the illusory person, and the true person are all three segments of the cessation of delusion through wisdom. When realized all at once, they are precisely peerless."
"Companions! Let us say: how is this single phrase at the tip of the staff? 'An iron hammer shatters golden bones.
Between heaven and earth, what is there? He then let out a shout and said, "There is no small amount of arrangement here."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The true lamp of the nightless dispels the night; the mind-moon pierces the day. This profound discourse is not of the sun; this wondrous instruction is beyond words.

A single phrase is perfectly clear, without traversing any tracks or paths. Try, I pray you, to speak of it. At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What is the mind-moon that dispels the night?
The Master replied, "It leaves no darkness behind. The monk asked, "What is the wondrous instruction that is not of the sun? The Master [replied]...

He said, "One does not dwell within the midst of clarity. The monk asked, "A single phrase is suddenly clear; it is difficult for tracks and paths to converge. At such a time as this, what is it like?
The Master struck him and said, "You have missed it, yet you do not even know it. The Master then said, "A single phrase cuts off the current;

ten thousand branches do not flow toward it. A thousand differences are severed at their paths; the three bodies are not obstructed. Sometimes clarity emerges from the dark; sometimes one enters the dark from within clarity."
"Darkness. [The Master] descended from his seat.
Zhuang said, "That which does not involve brightness or darkness is not yet the truth. Since brightness and darkness are fundamentally unreal, what can be taken as right?
You must practice for another thirty years."
