Record of Chan Master Zizhe of Lingzhu Jingci,
Volume Three (The Recorded Words and Explanations of Chan Master Mingzong of Shishuang).
Compiled by the junior monk of Wanshou Monastery, the bhikṣu Zankui Liao Guang. Opening the Hall:
A monk asked, "I recall the Great Master Bodhidharma saying: 'Externally, all conditions are stilled; internally, there is no breath.'"
"The mind is like a wall, for it can enter the Way. What do you make of this? The Master asked. The monk said, "Can you still comprehend it?
The Master replied, "Do you understand? The monk bowed. The Master said, "One who truly repays kindness. The monk asked, "But tell me, what mind does a wall have?
The Master said, "It is exactly like the mechanism of an iron ox. The monk said, "If that is so, then there is no way to recognize it? The Master said, "Speak quickly!"
"Quickly! The monk asked, "Can the Master speak? The Master said, "Your answer surpasses the functional application of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The monk said, "As expected, I am at fault. The Master said, "I, the old monk, am at fault. The Master then spoke this verse:
Externally, all conditions cease and speech is cut off; Internally, there is no breath, in accord with the profound mystery. The mind is like a wall—wherein effort is forgotten.
Entering the source of the Way prior to the kalpa of emptiness—Zhuangzi said:
"The mouth of the intoxicated man is at the edge of the world; the heart of the bright day is profound and mysterious. Clearly there are no traces;
deeply one forgets sages and worthies."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I recall Master Gushan saying: 'After the snow was cleared at Shaolin, Shen Guang realized it by severing his arm;

my humble way is full of frost upon the bed, yet there is not a single person who understands. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Only after the snow has been cleared can one begin to attain it.
The monk asked, "Does the Master also have a portion to share? The Master said, "This old fool has thirty [years' worth]."
"I excreted it years ago. The monk asked, "What is the matter now? The Master said, "Right on this seat, cold and chilly;
old bones, thin and frail. The Master then spoke a verse: A single turn of the mind’s light, And for a thousand miles, the realm of emotion is severed.
After awakening, after the dream has ended, I sit alone in the ancient hall.
Frost said: "Wisdom need not be transmitted through the mind; the barbarian monk has yet to master the verse. Gu Shan attained it spontaneously for himself;
his affection remains deep even after two lifetimes.
Ascending the hall, he was asked by a monk: "I recall the Great Master of Caoxi saying: 'Huineng has no special skills; he does not sever the hundred [senses]...'"
The monk said, "Thoughts arise toward objects; how can Bodhi grow? What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Already, you have developed clever artifice.
The monk asked, "How should a student understand this? The Master said, "The river water flows shallowly and is not turbid.
The monk asked, "What is this message? The Master said, "The green grass upon the riverbank is not withered. The monk said, "But what about..."
The student asked, "What is it that one should doubt and cling to? The Master said, "One who comes to speak of right and wrong is himself a person of right and wrong.
The Master then spoke this verse: "While young, one may exert effort; When old, one may let the mind rest. Now utterly weary of all affairs, My two eyes moisten my breast with tears."
The Frost said: "Old and young share the same heart through the endless years of cold; noble and base are separated by the lapels of their garments.
There is not a single point of skillful artifice, yet its value is worth a thousand pieces of gold. The waves of the Reed River surge upon the void; the fish of the Moss Sea swim in the depths."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I recall Master Yunmen saying: 'If you raise it and do not look back, you are immediately mistaken;
if you attempt to deliberate, when will you ever awaken? What is the meaning of this? The Master shouted and said: "A thousand years from now, you must avoid raising this too often!
The monk said: "But you are a descendant of Dayang; why such a manner of dealing with things? The Master said: [He remained silent.]

"Look! Within the flash of a stone striking fire, there is a path for emergence. The monk asked, "At what time? The Master struck the meditation seat. The monk bowed. The Master said, "A thousand errors.
He then spoke this verse: "Directly beneath, he thrusts aside Old Man Mu; Suddenly, he seizes the Elder Hao by the collar.
The spirit and bearing of the patch-robed monk lie beyond heaven and earth; One night, the cold ice reaches his entire body."
Shuang said: "If you can take it up at the very moment of the phrase, and if your words strike the mark, then provided you are earnest in heart and free from doubt, there is no harm in speaking;
even an iron-beaked bird might open its beak."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I recall Master Yunju saying, 'If you understand this, then Kāśyapa had nothing hidden;
if you do not understand this, then the World-Honored One has secret words. What is the meaning of this? The Master said:

"Hearing the Way of Confucius in the morning, one knows the filial piety of Laozi by evening. The monk said: "I do not ask about the Way of the Confucians; how about Śākyamuni? The Master said: [Silence].
The Master wished to remain without words, yet worldly dust would not allow him rest. The monk asked, "Setting aside for a moment whether one understands or not, what is the Tathāgata’s secret word?
The Master said, "Last night, the jade woman slept. The monk asked, "And as for the head-shaving ascetic (dhūta) smiling—what of that?"
The Master said, "Today, the Stone Man’s eyes are open. A monk asked, "Who knows this? The Master said, "Wrong, wrong.
The Master then spoke a verse: "The jade man sleeps deeply in the wondrous, clear pool; The Stone Man’s eyes open, and Flower Peak laughs. This is not a new awakening occurring today;
In the great certainty of three lifetimes, one surely knows it is not much."
Shuang said: "The black flower at midday; the green banana at midnight. After the wind-bone dream has cleared, the moon-mechanism emerges from the azure vines.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "I recall Master Ming’an saying: 'Do not guard the strange grasses turning green in the cold crags; sit..."
"The Quedai Baiyun school is not subtle; the matter of the guest and host is difficult to distinguish. When ruler and subject accord with the Way, there is laughter for ten thousand years.

What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "To sit firmly in one's position is not it; to fall into the realm of effort is not it. The monk asked, "When guest and host are difficult to distinguish, what then?
The Master said, "The old monk’s eyebrows are just like those of the Senior Monk (the questioner). The monk said, [and remained silent].
"How is it when ruler and minister are in accord with the Way? The Master said, "Internally and externally, they are fundamentally indistinguishable;
how can the orthodox and the deviant not be two? The monk asked, "Ultimately, how much do they differ? The Master said, "Pure light is fragrant wherever it goes;

the hidden birds call out in the bustle of spring. The Master then spoke this verse: "Once one attains the wondrous, A second time one forgets the wondrous. Hurry back! Clouds heaped upon clouds— White clouds."

Frost says: "In the heavens there is the Silver River; by the pond there are no iron flowers. Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī are old; what can one do about them?
At that moment of silence, a thousand years of error have since followed. Bad water splashed across the face—how cold!"

He addressed the assembly, saying: "In this place of mine, there is a thing. When you look for it, it is there; yet when you seek it, it is not. What is it?
Even so, it fills the eyes and ears, and is the hand-eye throughout the body. Therefore, the Sutra says:
'The pure physical eye born of one's parents sees the trichiliocosm. [Thus] he raises the banner of the Buddha’s universal radiance."
Having swept away the array of ordinary views that lack clarity, is there anyone who can prevail?

If you are a true man of great character, even if an iron wheel spins upon your head, your perfect illumination of concentration and wisdom will never be lost. If, however, you are still an unenlightened person, you must know that there is a separate way of life.
Out of compassion for you all, this mountain monk has raised his whisk and taken up his staff; yet, speaking according to reality, these are all—
This is a superfluous teaching. Ultimately, what is it? It has been thoroughly understood and discarded. Formerly, I mistakenly sought it along the road;
today, looking back, it is like ice within fire.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Vast and distant, yet without limit; luminous and pure, yet without stain.
This ground extends through all time, penetrating and transcending birth and death. Therefore it is said: 'When the mind-king does not move, the eight directions are open;

the pure manifestations are fundamentally undivided. Realizing the mystery, one is free from signs; profound and subtle, one is detached from form and partiality. Reaching this very point, there is no 'non-existence'."
Square. Not moving. Radiant and bright. As-it-is, dense and continuous. Do you see it? If you penetrate this thoroughly, I allow you to make it your livelihood.
If you have not yet done so, what can be done about the birth and death before your eyes? Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"If one awakens to the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, one is a true son of the Buddha. Those who claim to have attained what they have not attained shall incur the karma of hell. You must know this.
Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality; I, moreover, discuss reality and do not discuss emptiness. How, then, will you all thoroughly comprehend this?
If you wish to forget form and obliterate your traces, exert yourselves with earnest diligence in walking through space.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The samādhi of the patch-robed monks is such that their eyes look toward the southeast, while their intent lies toward the northwest;
it is entirely beyond the measurement of ordinary sentiments. When students apply effort, their minds are in a deep pool, casting the hook into the depths of the waves.
If you can realize this, the noble one ascends the dragon bed, and all rejoice at this auspicious moment. He alone awakens the teacherless, spontaneous wisdom; this right view is without proof."
This is all-encompassing wisdom. Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddhas mindfully regard sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not mindfully regard the Buddhas.

Only then do we know that when the Buddha delivers ordinary beings, it is the ordinary beings who deliver the Buddhas. At this point, dragons and snakes are intermingled, and ordinary people and sages dwell together.
Having entered the nature of the Dharma-realm, one observes the marks of the world alone; yet nature and marks are clearly manifest as non-dual. All you practitioners of dhyāna!
How can one deliberate upon this? Leaves fall because the wind is heavy; flowers droop because the dew is thick.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Among a thousand or ten thousand people, it is difficult to find even one person who has reached the ultimate limit of a single thought-moment.
Among ten thousand or a thousand people, it is difficult to encounter even one person who has thoroughly penetrated the profound source. Now tell me, why is it so?"
To seek only the branches and leaves while remaining ignorant of the roots and trunk—where does the fault lie? You have not yet understood the meaning of this moment from before;

today, look clearly at it for yourself. If there were a man who came forth to meet you, he would take up his seven-foot staff and wander freely through heaven and earth, with nothing at all to entangle his heels.
"A single patch-robed monk who has realized the matter—do you all yet act in this way? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The triple world is but the one mind;
outside the mind there are no separate dharmas. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
How can one attain such thorough penetration? The stars point north; the waters flow east.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "It is luminously clear and without partiality or crookedness; it is bright and possesses true illumination.
Even if one were to reach such a state through and through, it would still be merely an illumination that exists in isolation.

Only when the winds and waves have been extinguished within the ocean of the mind and one has reached the very bottom of the ocean of the Tathāgata-garbha (as-it-is) will one finally behold the pearl of the dragon. Do you understand? When there is complete understanding, there is nothing further to be known."
It is finished. At the point where the profound is most profound, one must simply revile it. These are the words of this mountain monk, who does not know good from bad;
before those with clear eyes, they cannot avoid being a source of laughter. How will you all comprehend this? The Sūtra says: "The Buddha-mind is inconceivable."
It is wondrous, beyond ordinary sentiment. If you can see in this way, you will attain a small measure of correspondence with it. Do you understand thoroughly?
The moon is bright in the high heavens; the water is cold in the dawn pool.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If this mountain monk were to encounter the teachers and monks of the present day—some raising a whisk or brandishing a staff to discourse on mind and nature;
some closing their rooms and silencing their speech to cut off both right and wrong; some roaming freely across the land, overturning meditation seats and shouting to disperse the great assembly;
or some concealing their own traces while reviling those from all quarters, and raising up other matters—what, after all, would that be?"
At this point, there is not the slightest use for logic; all such people are merely fabricating things.
Even so, since I am an old monk who happens to be "inside" [the matter], I am rightly subject to others' ridicule. How can I avoid this?
The ocean is naturally deep, and the mountain is naturally high.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "This single segment of the essential principle spans the present and illuminates the past, never lacking anything nor having any excess. In heaven it is identical to heaven; on earth it is identical to earth.
Its essence and function, guest and host, are everywhere sovereign. Entering the samādhi of spiritual powers and playful manifestation, one opens the dharma-gate of the great 'emptiness of falsehood.
Arriving here, one beholds the body of purple-polished gold—a single wisdom that is suchness, a single suchness."
The wisdom of wisdom. Thus the Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure; it is non-dual and without division, without distinction and without interruption.
O people, how can you see this and go beyond it? It is so, yet it is also not so; both "so" and "not so" are acceptable.
But ultimately, how do you thoroughly comprehend it? With the tip of a staff one lifts the sun and moon; within the palm one grasps [the universe].
Qiankun addressed the assembly, saying: "The moon is cold and sharp; the pond is bright and clear. Even if you practice in such a manner, you have not yet seen a dream of it.
It is the state where all traces of achievement are severed; it is precisely the hidden and secret ground. At this very moment, throughout one's entire being—"
In harmony with the Great Way. When the way of sovereign and subject is in accord, who can recognize it? In our family tradition, the dharma is subtly and perfectly manifest;
vast and expansive, they resonate in correspondence. Will you return to discern this? Wind and moon, a cold night—the crane’s dream is solitary.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "I see that the practitioners of the Way nowadays are entirely devoid of any semblance of true correspondence. Why is this so?
Whether they attempt to make the mind clear and still, or withdraw their thoughts to enter meditative absorption, they are all merely people engaged in artificial fabrication.
To speak according to reality, they are not at all the true masters within their own houses. If you wish to truly perceive this..."
A person must transform this mind that lacks the realization of the Way; how could there not be a distinction between those who have entrusted themselves to the teaching and those who have not?

Thus, a sutra says: "When a beginner bodhisattva enters samādhi, they have not yet eliminated the conceptual objects of that samādhi. Another sutra says: "When weary toil and deliberation are forever severed, one attains the purity of the dharma-realm;
yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to oneself. One must know that there is a profound mind and great virtue distinct from this—how can it be otherwise?
How can one attain such practice? Only when the merit of the white clouds is exhausted and one reaches the very summit of the green mountains, does one address the assembly, saying:
"The patch-robed monk has arrived by himself and seen by himself; he has reached the field of self-realization and personally beheld the natural state of abiding.
Only then, being there, is he one with that; being here, is he one with this. Thus, this and that correspond without [duality]."
The Section on Discernment: A desolate wind blows behind the houses; the pines before the temple rustle.
To act without a mind is spontaneous action, and this spontaneous action is itself naturally without a mind. Thus, a sutra says: "When the clouds move swiftly, the moon shifts;
when the boat travels, the shore seems to move. For what reason? The mountain clouds play lightly; the valley echoes are distant and profound. Whose realm is this? Examine it closely.
All of this is mere arrangement. But tell me, how does a monk beneath the paper robe conduct himself? When the clouds clear and the moon emerges, its light shines;

when the water cools, the pool conceals the pearl. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Penetrate beyond the three phrases; realize within the six lines. Pass straight through ten thousand layers of barriers."
One does not abide within the azure sky; first one must settle that side, and then one must practice on this side. Why?
If it were not for the matters of today, how could one speak of last night’s dream? Practice in this manner until you reach the ultimate, and you will be free and at ease.
If a monk has not yet attained this, what can he do when he receives an iron staff? Return to me the rice and gruel of my entire life! Therefore, the Sūtra says:
If you do not perceive the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you have not yet emerged from the realm of ordinary beings.

If you awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you do not depart from the triple world, yet you depart from greed, hatred, and delusion. When a single phrase is clearly realized, the Way is pointed out with distinct clarity; I grant you this as a great livelihood.
In the end, is it still thus? Public and private affairs are settled: the road to Chang’an.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma—every word contains the profound mystery, its resonance ever new.
If one raises a single scroll of this jade-bound volume, the nostrils of Gautama are grasped by everyone in their own hands.
If one takes up a single verse of its great meaning, the true eye of all Buddhas is entirely within each person’s heart. There is not a hair’s breadth of shift or change."
There is no leakage. Thus the Sūtra says: "All livelihoods and productive enterprises are entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*).
If it were so, all sentient beings on this great earth would simultaneously attain the Way and become Buddhas.
But tell me, who is it that acts in such a way? Three feet long in head, two inches short in neck.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The intent of the Teachings is to personally encounter [the Truth]; the intent of the Patriarchs is to arrive directly at it. The intent of the Patriarchs is to personally encounter [the Truth]; the intent of the Teachings is to arrive directly at it.
The Patriarchs and the Teachings are not two; their meaning and words are no different. Nevertheless, even though it is thus, one must truly reach this stage before it can be attained.

If you have not yet reached it, you must strictly avoid citing the Teachings or invoking the Patriarchs. How many people are there who truly know this point? Therefore, the Sutra says: 'In this assembly, there are none who possess branches.'"

"Only the true and substantial leaves remain; it would be well indeed if those of overweening pride were to retreat. If this is so, the path that leads upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages;
it is for those who have transcended [the mundane] to discern it. If the initial mind does not change, it remains identical to the subsequent mind."
Then why worry about not attaining it? Everyone must awaken. Among all Buddhas, those who have not yet realized are called sentient beings;
among sentient beings, those who have realized the ultimate meaning are called Buddhas. Therefore, the Great Master Bodhidharma said:

"Directly pointing at the human mind, seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha. At this very moment, what is it? It is the separate transmission outside the teachings, where no reliance is placed on words or letters.
[The Master] said: "When you have ultimately gone this way, how can you speak of it? The moon falls into the heart of the waves;
the azure pool is empty. He addressed the assembly, saying: "To the left they form a flock; to the right they form a troop.
Before one's face there is hemp; behind one is millet. Ultimately, what place is this? 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. Who says otherwise?"
Great Peace. This is precisely the time when [the Buddha] alone is honored; with valleys and ravines filled to the brim, where is there that is not a season of Great Peace?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Nature is inherently equal; there is no one who is equal. Thus the Patriarch said: "Mount Sumeru and Mount Cakravāḍa are all sealed by the One Dharma;
the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are all the manifestation of the body of the Ancient Buddha. How can this be otherwise?
He was permitted to depart. The moon hung above the treetops as dew moistened his robes.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "One must know that the three thousand worlds of the Buddha-land reside entirely within the single transformation of our Sovereign.

The dust and smoke of the four seas are cleansed; the six realms flourish as one family. Thus it is said: 'The Emperor’s power makes the mountains and peaks heavy; the Ruler’s grace is as deep as rain and dew. This is precisely so.
At such a time, a single *dharma*-flower meets spring once more; it is just like a lotus blooming in the month of December.
If you all wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season. When the time and season arrive, its principle will manifest of itself.
Why do you each fail to strive for its attainment? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Running in the morning and walking in the evening, there is nowhere one does not reach. You all—
"How does one discern the departure? Take up the Sumeru mallet and strike the drum of space," he said, showing the assembly:
"The ten-thousand-li long sky is without birth and without mind; the floating clouds have dispersed, and the great void is bright and clear.
Do you see this? If you can see it, I grant that you have repaid the Buddha's kindness. This message is that of the Buddhas of the three periods."
The ancestral masters of successive generations could not fully grasp it either. Why is this so? Do you understand? Even I, this mountain monk, cannot speak of it. For what reason?
Because the height of the mountain does not obstruct the drifting white clouds; the density of the bamboo does not hinder the flowing stream from passing through.
Now tell me, have you all grasped the essential point yet? Why do you not listen? At this point, even Bodhidharma did not understand. Great!
"How difficult, how very difficult!
He addressed the assembly, saying: "This very moment of resonance is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain's loftiness;
it is like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade's flawlessness. Reaching this point, there is no place for discernment, and no place for settling."

Cutting off all traces; cutting off all dependencies—this is the place where patch-robed monks arrive of their own accord, this is the place where students realize for themselves, this is the ground of the Buddhas of the three periods, and this is the ground of the six generations of patriarchs.
In each and every portion, there has never been any lack or deficiency. What is this? An ancient worthy said:
"A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its shadow sinks into the cold water; the goose has no intention of leaving a trace, yet the water..."

There is no heart that casts a shadow of stagnation. If one can be thus, this is true renunciation. Not yet; only by enduring the severe blows of the white staff will you attain a slight degree of correspondence with the Way.
Do you understand? A clear spring at Jinggu washes the white jade; the bright sun shines upon the pure river at Mount Taihua.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars—each polishes a mirror of antiquity and each washes away the idle slumber of the three remnants.
All of you, come meet me: do any of you possess the skillful means to polish that ancient mirror?"
"Great assembly! If there is anyone among you who can explain this, come forward; I shall bear witness for you. Alas!
From morning until evening, your mouths chatter incessantly, claiming this as right and that as wrong, without a moment's rest. What is the use of such things?"
They do nothing but eat their meals, drink their tea, keep their eyes open, and sleep-talk. Piteous are these dreamers who slumber; when will they ever wake up?
I respectfully submit this to those who practice the Way: time is to be cherished, the passing of the seasons flows like a stream, and the matter of birth and death is of the utmost gravity.
Impermanence is swift. Mountains collapse to form the sea; deep abysses transform into rapids. All phenomena are individually impermanent;

why do you not press forward and depart? Will you ever return? While this body of the five aggregates is still whole, you do not even recognize it; once the hundred bones have scattered, where will you seek it?
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In such a state, acting in such a way—when one reaches this, it is wondrous; when one arrives at this, it is profound.
To shift it aside and turn it open is the place where a patch-robed monk turns his body and the entrance through which all of you awaken.
Do you see it? If you wish to see, see it immediately; do not hesitate to deliberate. If you can shift it aside here, I grant that you possess the true eye. As for that which is not so..."
When it is not thus, the Buddhas of the three periods cannot speak of it, and the Patriarchs of the six generations cannot lift it up.
Reaching this point, it is suchness upon suchness, profound mystery within profound mystery; one must take it up and shoulder it through to the very top and the very bottom.
If one can do so, one is a man who cannot be held back. How can there be both "thus" and "not thus"?
The fundamental principle: it departs from the place where ten thousand autumns dwell amidst the clouds, yet returns to the edge of the myriad waters upon the river.
Is there still anyone who understands? A single point right across the head—do not say you have not heard it.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "When the single aperture pointing upward is opened wide, all the sages alike fall beneath its influence. Upon reaching this state, whether to tear it asunder or to close it together is up to me.

For one who realizes that heaven and earth share a single root and all things are of one body, at such a time they may plant their feet across other worlds or shift their person to the summit of Mount Sumeru; sometimes they sit upon the Bodhi tree."
Beneath the tree, he opens the Vajra-eye; at times on the slopes of Mount Cakravāḍa, he sharpens his adamantine ear.
Tell me, what kind of countenance does this man possess? Deliberate upon this carefully. Why is it that his entire being is so vividly present and his whole person so clearly manifest?
Ultimately, how is it? Śākyamuni is in front; Maitreya is behind.

When the Master first went to visit Chan Master Hongzhi of Tiantong, he asked: "What is the wondrous flavor upon the tongue? Hongzhi—
[Zhizang] said, "This is the gate of ambrosia. The Master asked, "Does it still have coming and going?
Zhizang said, "Coming and going are not obstructed. The Master asked, "Why is it in everyone's mouth? Zhizang said, "The subtlety of seeing and hearing transcends both sound and form.
The Master then prostrated. Zhizang asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The Master said, "Does the Master not know? Zhizang said, "For now, stay here."
They conversed within, and the Master then returned to his guest quarters. From that time on, he remained in attendance for seventeen years.
When [the abbot] went from Tiantong to Changlu, he invited the Master to serve as the Head Seat; all the assembly marveled at this.
The Master went to Mount Jing to see Master Liao. He asked, "A frog at the bottom of the well swallows the moon;

at the third watch, one does not borrow the 'night-bright' curtain. What is the meaning of this? Liao replied, "Can you still fathom it? The Master said, "I am but a person born of parents; how could I blame you, Master?
Liao said, "You have come to meet a true master in person. The Master then prostrated himself. Liao... [said: "... (The Master then departed.)
He said, "Today I have finally encountered the poisonous hand of a man.
Thereupon, the Master went to Da Hong to see Master Xian, who asked, "The sages of all generations have never spoken of this for the sake of others."
"How about you, Master? Xian said, "I am also like this. The Master said, "What can be done about this? Xian said, "Leave it to him to resent it.
The Master said, "If that is so, does the student have no share in it? Xian said, "Just sit and drink some tea.
The Master asked, "What kind of mental activity is this? Xian laughed heartily. The Master then prostrated himself.
The Master went to Shimen and saw Master Cong, who asked him, "After reaching the single breath, when the function is received before the mind, how is it?
Cong said, "You have missed it. The Master said, "Did the Master miss it, or did I miss it?
Cong said, "It is the old monk's fault. The Master then bowed. Cong said, "He does not accept people's bows. The Master said, "..."
"What do you mean? Cong smiled in agreement.
The Master then went to Yunju to see West Monk (Xishi). He asked, "I have also heard that you, Master, do not understand Zen;
is this true or not? Yunju said, "It is. The Master asked, "Why do you not understand? Yunju remained silent. The Master then returned and understood.
In the guest quarters, the Abbot sent an attendant to deliver this verse: "Yunju does not understand Zen; He washes his feet and climbs onto his bed to sleep.
Unaware that his pillow has fallen, He breaks the monastery’s brick. The Master opened the door and saw him, then offered this reply:
"The Abbot does not understand Zen; When weary, he simply beats upon his pillow and sleeps. A clay ox eats water and grass; A wooden horse bites a tile-brick. The attendant took [the verse] and...
The verse was presented to Xixi. Xixi asked, "What is this? As the attendant was about to open his mouth, Xixi struck him.
At that moment, the attendant suddenly attained great enlightenment. When the Master (Linji) heard of this, he said, "It is a pity that such a painful blow was let go."
The Master went to Mount Jiangshan to see Master Zhao, who asked him, "Since there is no dharma of awakening to be attained, why is there the transmission of the Dharma?
Zhao said, "Because there is no dharma of awakening. The Master asked, "Where does it then fall? Zhao said, "Go and drink tea."
The Master said, "You still have not escaped the hardship of the golden lock. Deshan then ceased speaking and bowed.
Thereupon, the Master went to Fayun to see Master Xian. Xian asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come directly from Zu."
The immortal asked, "How many people are under your guidance? The Master made a gesture of stepping forward. The immortal said, "You have missed it, yet you do not even realize it.
The Master said, "As expected, as expected.
Thereupon, the Master went to Jia Shan to see Master Qin, who asked, "Have you received the Buddha-dharma of Linji until now?"
Dwelling on this mountain, what is the eye that belongs to one’s own house? [Zhaozhou] called out in a vigorous tone and then let out a shout.
The Master said, "I have been shouted at by the Abbot. Qian said, "Who do you see coming? The Master said, "The Abbot Jue of Tiantong.
Qian said, "In that case, you are not a master. The Master again called out in a vigorous tone and then let out a shout. Qian said, "A true lion cub; he can roar like a lion."
"Hou! The Master shook his sleeves and went out.
Later, the Master went to Xuefeng to see Master Ru. Ru asked, "Where have you come from, you traveler passing by?
The Master replied, "I have come from Tiantong. Ru asked, "What have you brought with you? The Master made a gesture of inspection and said, "Look. Ru said, "You have been seen through."
Linji said, "Exposed! Exposed! As if striking a palm, he said, "The grass-thief is utterly defeated. Linji said, "This is an old thief.
As if saying, "Tiantong, what words do you have to show to your disciples? Linji said, "How about you, Master? As if saying, "Your thieving mind has not yet been eliminated."
The Master said, "Indeed, indeed. If you can return a single phrase to me," the Master then prostrated himself.
Thereupon, the Master went to Lingyin to see the Venerable Xinghe, who asked, "What is the family tradition of Dongshan? Xinghe replied:
"Neither the partial nor the primary ever departs from its original station; how could non-arising involve the causes and conditions of speech?
The Master said, "This is a matter of peripheral study. What is the phrase that points directly upward? Xing said, "Do you not see him walking among those of different species?
The Master then prostrated himself. Xing said, "Is it not walking among those of different species? The Master then smiled and departed. Xing said, "Wait a moment..."
He was drinking tea there when he went to see Master Chan at Yuyang.
Chan asked, "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, "Lingyin. Chan asked, "Have you seen Zen Master Xing?
The Master recounted the previous conversation. Chan said, "There is nothing that prevents you from being evasive and circuitous."
"The old monk constantly employs this kind of expedient. Others are unwilling to accept it. The Master asked, "Who is this person?
As Chan was about to open his mouth, the Master said, "He is already an outsider. Chan involuntarily stuck out his tongue. The Master said, "Please offer the Master one or two cases."
Chan said, "When meeting those who understand, they are rare. The Master asked, "If someone were to ask you this, how would you respond?
Chan remained silent. The Master then paid his respects.
The Master went to Mount Jinshan to see Master Qing and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

Qing replied, "This is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master asked, "Is there not another phrase? Qing said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. The Master said, "I am ashamed.
Qing asked, "Who has received and transmitted the wondrous secret of Shaolin? The Master replied, "It does not fall [into categories]."
Jiaojing asked, "Qing, what do you say? The Master said, "This is a matter of spiritual practice. Qing said, "Right, right.
The Master said, "Thank you for your response."
The Master went to Yungai to see Master Ling. Ling asked, "Where have you come from, monk? The Master replied, "I recently left Jinshan.
Ling asked, "How is the Dharma-way at Jinshan? The Master spread out both hands. Ling asked, "What message is this?"
The Master bowed and said, "The Master does not recognize characters. Ling said, "I thank you for providing an answer.
The Master said, "There is no lack of gratitude, but what can one do about that [other thing]? Ling said, "Can you bring forth that other thing? The Master departed with a clear, composed air.
Ling said, "It is not it, it is not it. The Master did not speak again.
The Master went to Kaifu to see Master Ning and asked, "What is one's original face before one's parents were born?
Ning replied, "You are a Chan practitioner. The Master said, "Of what use is that? Ning said, "There is a large flat stone on the steps below.
The Master then prostrated himself. Ning said, "Attendant, bring some tea for this honored guest."
The Master raised his voice and let out a shout. Ning asked, "Why use a thief? The Master said, "You must go drink tea. Ning said, "I am at fault.
Ning then returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master subsequently went to Daci to see Master Ying. When Ying saw the Master approaching, he sat facing the wall. The Master then struck the attendant three times with his palm.
The attendant laughed loudly, "He-he. The Master said, "When one's insight is equal to the teacher's, it diminishes the teacher's virtue by half."
"Only one whose wisdom surpasses that of the master is fit to receive the transmission. Yì asked this with great precision and propriety, yet the attendant remained silent.
The following day, as they returned, the Master said, "A fellow who has the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake. Yì replied, "Even so, let us deliberate upon it carefully.
The Master said, "Once seen, there is no need to see it again. Yì said, "That is too crude. The Master asked, "And what about you, Master? After a long silence, Yì spoke.
The Master pushed him out and threw him down. The following day, he remarked, "In thirty years, I have never encountered such a master.
Thereupon, the Master went to see Master Ming at Baizhang. Ming said, "This mountain is steep and precipitous;
no one can reach it. Why have you managed to get here? The Master replied, "I simply came because I knew there was a Master three thousand *li* away. Ming said:
"This thatched-roof hut is what this old monk uses. The Master said, "I fear it still lingers on your lips. Ming said, "Wrong.
The Master said, "Out of compassion, Master, grant me one word. Ming said, "Wrong. The Master said, "Wrong, wrong. Ming then returned to the abbot's quarters.
The Master then went out. Ming again sent an attendant, saying, "It is already somewhat late today; please stay for one night.

He then asked his fellow student, "How far is the road to Xuefeng? The student replied, "It is over one hundred li; there are many dangers along the way.
Do you wish to go there? If you do, I must escort you. The Master said, "Very well, very well. He then went to the place of Chan Master Qi.
Upon seeing the Master arrive, Qi asked, "How extraordinary! Last night I dreamed of a *maitreya*..."
The Master came to my quarters and said, "The Abbot is a dragon nesting in a phoenix’s lair; I am a phoenix nesting in a dragon’s lair. We must be of one kind.
Unconsciously, I prostrated myself before him. Today, seeing you, I find you to be truly extraordinary. From this point on, you shall remain here with me.
Nineteen years later, he again spoke in accord with me, saying, "Your karmic conditions and affairs do not lie here. For now, you may go."
He departed for Tiantong. Now, Master Zhengjue was flourishing there with a following already exceeding a thousand; if you were to go there, you would be fit to occupy the position of First Seat.
The Master then followed Chijiao’s instructions and went to Tiantong; their exchange of questions and answers is recorded in the preceding chapter.
The Master then occupied the first seat, and the entire assembly regarded him with great esteem. He followed Zen Master Hongzhi for seventeen years.
Zen Master Wukong of Mount Jing was his master’s uncle, while Venerable Tiantong Jué was his master’s teacher;
together they served as witnesses. Having received the seal of transmission from these two masters, he set out on his travels.
In his later years, he visited twenty-five venerable elders. Subsequently, he returned to Tiantong and accepted the invitation from Jingci Monastery.
He entered the monastery on the twenty-fifth day of the second month of the twenty-fifth year of the Shaoxing era.
He retired from the monastery on the nineteenth day of the seventh month of the twenty-sixth year. The Master served as a monk for sixty-eight years. [The following] is extracted from therein:
In the world, she lived for twelve years; at seventy, she passed away.
She had come forth having shaved her hair at the age of eleven, and she never once visited a nunnery or a hermitage. Her body was pure, like the moon reflected in water.
The Master read and examined one hundred and twenty thousand scrolls of sutras, śāstras, and other books, yet no one knew the reason why. [This was witnessed by] the layman Yutian, Cong.
The layman Lin and the layman Youpu were both among the great protectors; they served as assistants when the Master appeared in the world.
There were thirteen people who followed him as dharma heirs and appeared in the world, with Shishuang Zong and Donggu Guang at their head.
The assembly of monks under his guidance numbered more than seven hundred. Although there were many venerable elders from all quarters, [he was] peerless under heaven.
Below, Master Shi (Shenxiu) recommended him, saying: "He encompasses both the internal and external completely; the rest is unfathomable. This is truly Mahābrahmā.
Emperor [Gaozong] bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Zide; this was indeed an imperial posthumous name. Wang Chi has recorded the general outline of the Master’s life in his *Guǎngzhōng zǐ*.
Is it not the case that nine-tenths or eight-tenths of its essential meaning cannot be reached? The inscription says:
"The ancestral hall is radiant, illuminating the subtle purity of Shaolin; the lineage of the fundamental teaching continues the spiritual mystery of Xinfeng."
The Buddha’s radiance shines brilliantly, bearing the essence of Vulture Peak; the Zen groves flourish luxuriantly, revealing the harmonious intent of Tiantong.
The rhinoceros horn transmits its vital breath—congratulations on this universal peace; the phoenix’s beak produces its form, establishing the three sections of essential sincerity.

Having personally received the Dharma from Master Zide, he succeeded to the hundred-year legacy of Hongzhi. He inherited the secret applications transmitted within his own house and upheld the thousand-year practice of Dayang.
The Master has traversed seventy years of the human flower; how could his subsequent deeds ever be fully captured by the subtle refinements of words and thought?
